question: The practice of Sati was prohibited in 1829 by which Governor-General, with the efforts of Raja Ram Mohan Roy?
solution_text:
The correct answer is William Bentinck.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• William Bentinck declared Sati illegal through Regulation XVII of 1829, after a campaign by Raja Ram Mohan Roy (राजा राममोहन राय के प्रयास से बेंटिक ने 1829 में सती प्रथा पर रोक लगाई)

 

• The ban was first applied in Bengal and then extended to Bombay and Madras Presidencies in 1830.

 

• Such social reforms, together with the Widow Remarriage Act of 1856, were viewed by orthodox sections as interference with religion and are listed among the social causes of the Revolt.

 

• Bentinck's term (1828-35) also saw the suppression of the Thugs and the introduction of English as the medium of higher education.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Raja Ram Mohan Roy founded the Brahmo Samaj in 1828.

 

• The Revolt took place almost three decades after the ban.

 

• Bentinck was the last Governor-General of Bengal and the first Governor-General of India.

 

• The 1829 regulation made Sati punishable as culpable homicide, and Raja Ram Mohan Roy later travelled to England, where he died at Bristol in 1833.

 

NOTE

 

• Lord Hastings (Option 1): Lord Hastings (1813-23) was occupied with the Anglo-Nepal and Pindari wars and the Maratha settlement, and did not abolish Sati, which was a feature of Bentinck's later administration.

 

• Lord Dalhousie (Option 3): Lord Dalhousie governed from 1848 to 1856 and is associated with the Doctrine of Lapse, railways and the telegraph, not with the abolition of Sati in the 1820s.

 

• Lord Ripon (Option 4): Lord Ripon was Viceroy from 1880 to 1884, after the Revolt, and is known for local self-government; he could not have banned Sati in 1829.

question:
Arrange the following events in chronological order (earliest first):

1. Widow Remarriage Act is passed

2. Annexation of Awadh

3. Mangal Pandey attacks British officers at Barrackpore

4. Sepoys rise at Meerut
solution_text:
The correct answer is 2, 1, 3, 4.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Awadh was annexed by Dalhousie in February 1856 on the charge of misgovernance, which makes it the earliest of the four (अवध का विलय 1856 के आरंभ में हुआ)

 

• The Widow Remarriage Act was passed under Canning in July 1856, after Awadh and before the sepoy unrest of 1857.

 

• Mangal Pandey attacked Lt. Baugh and Sergeant-Major Hewson at Barrackpore on 29 March 1857.

 

• The formal outbreak followed at Meerut on 10 May 1857, so the correct sequence is 2, 1, 3, 4.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The two 1856 events show how political and social grievances built up before the military spark of 1857.

 

• Berhampur's refusal in February 1857 comes before Barrackpore but is not among the events listed here.

 

• Delhi fell to the rebels on 12 May 1857 and was recaptured on 20 September 1857.

 

NOTE

 

• 1, 2, 3, 4 (Option 2): Placing the Widow Remarriage Act before the annexation of Awadh is wrong, because Awadh was taken in February 1856 while the Act was passed in the middle of that year, in July.

 

• 2, 3, 1, 4 (Option 3): Putting Mangal Pandey's attack before the Widow Remarriage Act reverses the order; the Act of 1856 precedes the Barrackpore incident of March 1857 by many months.

 

• 1, 3, 2, 4 (Option 4): Starting with the Act and then Mangal Pandey before Awadh is incorrect, as the annexation of Awadh was the first event and the Act followed it within 1856.

question:
Arrange the following events of 1857-59 in chronological order (earliest first):

1. Capture of Delhi by the British

2. Rani Laxmi Bai dies in battle

3. Queen Victoria's Proclamation

4. Execution of Tantia Tope
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2, 3, 4.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The British recaptured Delhi on 20 September 1857 under John Nicholson, the earliest event (दिल्ली पर 20 सितंबर 1857 को पुनः अधिकार)

 

• Rani Laxmi Bai died as a soldier on 17 June 1858 at Gwalior, after Jhansi had fallen to Hugh Rose in April.

 

• Queen Victoria's Proclamation was read at Allahabad on 1 November 1858, announcing the end of Company rule.

 

• Tantia Tope was betrayed, captured and hanged in April 1859, the last of the four, giving the order 1, 2, 3, 4.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• After 1 November 1858, Lord Canning became the first Viceroy.

 

• Tantia Tope's execution marks the effective end of organised resistance of the Revolt.

 

• Bahadur Shah Zafar was deported to Rangoon in 1858 and died in 1862.

 

• Rani Laxmi Bai's death and the Proclamation are separated by about five months, while Tantia Tope was betrayed by Man Singh of Narwar and executed at Shivpuri in April 1859.

 

NOTE

 

• 2, 1, 3, 4 (Option 1): Putting the Rani's death before the fall of Delhi is wrong, since Delhi fell in September 1857, while the Rani died in June 1858, nine months afterwards.

 

• 1, 3, 2, 4 (Option 2): Placing the Proclamation before the Rani's death is incorrect, because the Rani died on 17 June 1858 and the Queen's declaration was issued only on 1 November 1858.

 

• 1, 2, 4, 3 (Option 3): Tantia Tope was executed in April 1859, after the Proclamation of November 1858, so placing his execution third reverses the true order of the last two events.

question: Which Indian nationalist hailed the Revolt of 1857 as the 'First War of Indian Independence'?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Vinayak Damodar Savarkar.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• V.D. Savarkar called the Revolt the First War of Indian Independence in his book written in 1907-08 and published in 1909 (सावरकर ने 1857 को प्रथम स्वतंत्रता संग्राम कहा)

 

• He rejected the British description of the rising as a mere 'sepoy mutiny' and presented it as a national uprising.

 

• His view contrasts with Sir John Lawrence, who regarded it as a purely military outbreak and not a conspiracy to overthrow British rule.

 

• R.C. Majumdar disagreed with both, holding that it was neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Savarkar's book was banned by the British before it was widely published.

 

• S.N. Sen's study of the Revolt is considered an official history of 1857 commissioned in the 1950s.

 

• Savarkar later became a prominent Hindu Mahasabha leader.

 

• Savarkar wrote the work in Marathi in 1907, partly in London, and its English translation was circulated secretly; he was also arrested in 1910 and sentenced to transportation to the Andamans.

 

NOTE

 

• Jawaharlal Nehru (Option 1): Jawaharlal Nehru wrote in The Discovery of India that the Revolt was more than a mutiny, but the label 'First War of Indian Independence' is credited to Savarkar.

 

• Bipin Chandra Pal (Option 2): Bipin Chandra Pal was a Lal-Bal-Pal Extremist leader of the Swadeshi era, and he is not the author of the 1909 work that described 1857 as a war of independence.

 

• Gopal Krishna Gokhale (Option 4): Gopal Krishna Gokhale was a Moderate leader and founder of the Servants of India Society, and he did not write the account that gave 1857 this name.

question: Which historian held that the so-called 'First National War of Independence' was neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence?
solution_text:
The correct answer is R.C. Majumdar.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• R.C. Majumdar argued that the Revolt was neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence, since earlier revolts had occurred and the rising did not cover the whole country (आर.सी. मजूमदार का मत)

 

• He pointed out that large parts of India, as well as many Indian rulers, landlords and the educated middle class, did not support the rebels.

 

• Savarkar, on the other hand, called it the First War of Indian Independence.

 

• John Lawrence saw it as a purely military outbreak, not a conspiracy against British rule, while S.N. Sen thought it part of the struggle for independence.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Majumdar co-authored the volume on the Sepoy Mutiny and Revolt of 1857.

 

• Earlier uprisings such as the Vellore Mutiny of 1806 and tribal revolts predate 1857.

 

• Debates on the character of 1857 are still a standard topic of historiography.

 

• R.C. Majumdar edited the multivolume History and Culture of the Indian People and argued that the sepoy rising lacked a common ideology or leadership extending beyond the army.

 

NOTE

 

• S.N. Sen (Option 2): S.N. Sen argued that the rising was part of the struggle for independence, which is the opposite of Majumdar's conclusion that it was not a war of independence at all.

 

• V.D. Savarkar (Option 3): Savarkar hailed the Revolt as the First War of Indian Independence, so he stands against the denial of its national character that Majumdar made.

 

• John Lawrence (Option 4): John Lawrence saw it as purely a military mutiny rather than a conspiracy to overthrow British rule; his claim concerns the mutiny's nature and not the three-fold denial quoted.

question:
Match the historian/figure with the view on the Revolt of 1857:

Historian: (a) John Lawrence (b) V.D. Savarkar (c) R.C. Majumdar (d) S.N. Sen

View: (i) First War of Indian Independence (ii) Neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence (iii) A purely military outbreak, not a conspiracy (iv) Part of the struggle for independence
solution_text:
The correct answer is a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• John Lawrence saw the rising as a purely military outbreak rather than a conspiracy to overthrow British rule, so (a) matches (iii) (जॉन लॉरेंस - केवल सैनिक विद्रोह)

 

• V.D. Savarkar hailed it as the First War of Indian Independence, so (b) matches (i).

 

• R.C. Majumdar held it was neither first, nor national, nor a war of independence, so (c) matches (ii).

 

• S.N. Sen regarded the Revolt as part of the struggle for independence, so (d) matches (iv); this leaves the combination a-iii, b-i, c-ii, d-iv.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Lawrence's view reflects the official British reading that the trouble was confined to the army.

 

• Sen's book Eighteen Fifty-Seven was published in 1957, the centenary year.

 

• The word 'mutiny' implies a revolt of soldiers, while 'revolt' or 'war' suggests wider participation.

 

• Other views include Disraeli's 'national revolt', Outram and Taylor's 'Hindu-Muslim conspiracy', and the Marxist reading of a peasant uprising against feudal and colonial exploitation.

 

NOTE

 

• a-i, b-iii, c-ii, d-iv (Option 1): This option gives Lawrence the view that it was the First War of Independence and Savarkar the military-outbreak view, which reverses what each of them actually argued.

 

• a-iii, b-i, c-iv, d-ii (Option 2): Here Majumdar is given the 'part of the struggle' view and Sen the 'neither first nor national' view, swapping the two historians whose conclusions point in opposite directions.

 

• a-ii, b-i, c-iii, d-iv (Option 3): In this arrangement Lawrence is credited with Majumdar's denial, and Majumdar with the military-outbreak view, which wrongly interchanges two distinct interpretations of 1857.

question: Who was the British Prime Minister at the time of the Revolt of 1857?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lord Palmerston.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Lord Palmerston was the British Prime Minister in 1857, while Canning was the Governor-General of India (पामर्स्टन 1857 में ब्रिटेन के प्रधानमंत्री थे)

 

• His government dealt with the crisis in India and passed the Act of 1858 that transferred the administration of India to the Crown.

 

• Bahadur Shah II was the Mughal emperor around whom the rebels rallied.

 

• The three offices together - Palmerston in London, Canning in Calcutta and Bahadur Shah in Delhi - are the key figures noted for this chapter.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• Palmerston served as Prime Minister in 1855-58 and again in 1859-65.

 

• Disraeli, though not Prime Minister then, described the rising as a national revolt in Parliament.

 

• The Act for the Better Government of India was passed in August 1858.

 

• Palmerston was a Liberal Prime Minister whose ministry fell in 1858 over the Orsini affair, and the India Bill was then introduced by the Conservative government of Lord Derby.

 

NOTE

 

• William Gladstone (Option 2): William Gladstone first became Prime Minister in 1868, more than a decade after the Revolt, so he was not heading the government in 1857.

 

• Benjamin Disraeli (Option 3): Benjamin Disraeli first became Prime Minister briefly in 1868 and again in 1874-80; in 1857 he sat in opposition, and later commented that it was a national revolt.

 

• Robert Peel (Option 4): Robert Peel was Prime Minister in 1834-35 and 1841-46 and died in 1850, so he could not have headed the government when the Revolt took place.

question: Who was the Governor-General of India when the Revolt of 1857 broke out?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Lord Canning.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Lord Canning was the Governor-General from 1856 and held office throughout the Revolt, later becoming the first Viceroy (1857 के विद्रोह के समय गवर्नर-जनरल लॉर्ड कैनिंग थे)

 

• He had succeeded Dalhousie in February 1856, a few months before the outbreak, and the Widow Remarriage Act of 1856 was enacted under him.

 

• His policy of restraint toward the rebels after the suppression earned him the nickname 'Clemency Canning'.

 

• Under the Queen's Proclamation of 1858 he became the first Viceroy of India.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Canning also introduced the General Service Enlistment Act of 1856, which required sepoys to serve overseas if needed.

 

• He established the universities of Calcutta, Bombay and Madras in 1857.

 

• The Indian Councils Act of 1861 was passed during his Viceroyalty.

 

• Canning's governor-generalship (1856-62) also saw the Indian Councils Act of 1861, which began associating Indians with the legislature and restored the Presidency governments' legislative powers.

 

NOTE

 

• Lord Dalhousie (Option 1): Lord Dalhousie left India in February 1856, before the Revolt; his policies such as the Doctrine of Lapse contributed to the causes, but he was no longer in office in 1857.

 

• Lord Lawrence (Option 2): John Lawrence was Chief Commissioner of Punjab in 1857 and became Viceroy only in 1864; he was not the Governor-General at the time the Revolt broke out.

 

• Lord Ripon (Option 3): Lord Ripon was Viceroy from 1880 to 1884, more than two decades after the Revolt, and has no role in the events of 1857.

question: After the Revolt of 1857, the post of the Governor-General of India was redesignated as:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Viceroy of India.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Under the Government of India Act, 1858 the Governor-General became the Viceroy of India, the Crown's direct representative, with Canning as the first holder (गवर्नर-जनरल का पद वायसराय बना)

 

• Company rule ended and Crown rule began after Queen Victoria's declaration of 1858.

 

• A Secretary of State for India, a member of the British cabinet, took over the work of the Board of Control and the Court of Directors.

 

• The Doctrine of Lapse was abolished and the British pledged non-interference in Indian social and religious matters.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Secretary of State was assisted by a Council of India with fifteen members.

 

• The title Viceroy was the personal representative of the monarch, while the Governor-General remained the legal title for official acts.

 

• Queen Victoria became Empress of India in 1876.

 

• The Viceroy ruled with an Executive Council, while the Secretary of State for India in London held the supreme authority and consulted a council of fifteen members.

 

NOTE

 

• Secretary of State for India (Option 1): The Secretary of State for India was a minister in London who headed the India Office; the Governor-General was not given that title but the resident Viceroy's rank.

 

• Governor of Bengal (Option 3): Governor of Bengal was a provincial post under the Governor-General and then the Viceroy, so the highest officer in India was not reduced to that rank.

 

• Commander-in-Chief (Option 4): The Commander-in-Chief was the army's head, a separate office, and Canning's civil post did not become a military appointment after the Revolt.

question: The rule of the East India Company in India ended and Crown rule began through:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Queen Victoria's declaration of 1858.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Government of India Act, 1858 and Queen Victoria's Proclamation of the same year ended the Company's rule and transferred India to the Crown (1858 की घोषणा से कंपनी शासन समाप्त हुआ)

 

• The Revolt convinced Parliament that the Company could no longer govern India, and the Crown assumed direct responsibility.

 

• The Governor-General was designated Viceroy, and the Doctrine of Lapse was withdrawn.

 

• The British promised not to interfere in the social and religious matters of Indians and extended to the princes a guarantee of their rights.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Proclamation was read at a durbar in Allahabad on 1 November 1858.

 

• The Board of Control and Court of Directors were abolished.

 

• The Queen's Proclamation promised equal treatment and admission to services irrespective of race or creed.

 

• The Act for the Better Government of India (1858) was passed in August 1858, and the Board of Control and Court of Directors were abolished, so the Company's existence ended on paper too.

 

NOTE

 

• Pitt's India Act of 1784 (Option 1): Pitt's India Act of 1784 created the Board of Control to supervise the Company, which meant the Company continued to govern; it preceded the Revolt by 73 years.

 

• Regulating Act of 1773 (Option 2): The Regulating Act of 1773 was the first parliamentary attempt to regulate the Company's affairs and created the Governor-General of Bengal post; it did not end Company rule.

 

• Charter Act of 1833 (Option 4): The Charter Act of 1833 ended the Company's trade monopoly and made the Governor-General of India; the Company still ruled afterwards, so this did not cause Crown rule.

question: Queen Victoria's Proclamation announcing the transfer of India to the Crown was read out in 1858 at:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Allahabad.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Lord Canning read the Queen's Proclamation at a durbar at Allahabad on 1 November 1858, announcing the end of Company rule (इलाहाबाद में 1 नवंबर 1858 को महारानी की घोषणा पढ़ी गई)

 

• The Proclamation promised respect for the rights and customs of Indian princes, and an end to annexations on the pretext of the Doctrine of Lapse.

 

• It also pledged non-interference in religion, and equal and impartial admission to public services.

 

• Allahabad served as the seat of the North-Western Provinces government at the time, which made it a suitable choice.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Allahabad later hosted the 1888 Congress session and became the home of the Anand Bhawan.

 

• Canning's durbar was a state occasion in which Indian rulers were told that their territory would be respected.

 

• The Proclamation is sometimes called the 'Magna Carta' of the Indian people.

 

• The Proclamation recognised Indian princes' rights, promised to respect their dignity, and offered pardon to all rebels not guilty of killing British subjects, aiming at reconciliation after the war.

 

NOTE

 

• Calcutta (Option 1): Calcutta was the seat of the Governor-General and the capital of British India, but the Proclamation was publicly proclaimed at a durbar in Allahabad.

 

• Delhi (Option 3): Delhi had just been recaptured in 1857 and was placed under the Punjab administration; the Queen's declaration of 1858 was not read out there.

 

• Bombay (Option 4): Bombay was one of the three presidencies, and it did not host the durbar at which Canning communicated the Queen's declaration to the people of India.

question:
Consider the following statements about the results of the Revolt of 1857:

1. The Doctrine of Lapse was abolished.

2. The British pledged not to interfere in social and religious matters of Indians.

3. The Governor-General's post was renamed Viceroy of India.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1, 2 and 3.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: the Doctrine of Lapse was withdrawn after the Revolt, and the right of adoption was accepted (व्यपगत सिद्धांत समाप्त किया गया)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: the Proclamation of 1858 promised non-interference in the religion and social customs of Indians.

 

• Statement 3 is correct: the Governor-General became the Viceroy of India, with Canning as the first Viceroy.

 

• Since all three statements are true, the correct choice is 1, 2 and 3; the Revolt also ended Company rule and ushered in Crown rule.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The army was reorganised so that the proportion of European soldiers increased, and artillery was kept in British hands.

 

• The Indian princes were recognised as loyal allies and were treated as a bulwark of British rule.

 

• The Revolt's failure, with Hindu-Muslim unity as a gain, fostered a sense of patriotism.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 2 only (Option 1): Excluding the Viceroy statement is wrong, because the post of Governor-General was redesignated Viceroy of India after the Revolt, with Canning as the first holder.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 2): Excluding the Doctrine of Lapse statement is wrong, since the doctrine was abolished after 1857 and adoption by Indian rulers was recognised in the Proclamation.

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 4): Dropping the non-interference pledge is wrong, because the British promised in the Queen's Proclamation not to interfere in Indian social and religious matters after 1858.

question: Which of the following was NOT a cause of the Revolt of 1857?
option_4: The greased cartridges of the Enfield rifle
solution_text:
The correct answer is The Vernacular Press Act, 1878.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Vernacular Press Act was passed in 1878 under Lord Lytton, twenty-one years after the Revolt, and therefore could not be a cause (1878 का वर्नाक्यूलर प्रेस एक्ट 1857 के बाद का है)

 

• The annexation of Awadh in 1856 was a political cause, and it angered the sepoys and taluqdars.

 

• The Doctrine of Lapse of Dalhousie annexed states like Jhansi and Satara and was a political cause.

 

• The greased cartridges of the Enfield rifle were the religious cause and the immediate spark.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Vernacular Press Act aimed to control Indian-language newspapers and was repealed under Ripon in 1882.

 

• The Revolt had economic, social, religious, political and military causes.

 

• Sepoys' grievances on pay, promotion and batta were military causes.

 

• Other causes are the economic ruin of artisans and peasants under heavy taxation and the racial arrogance of the British, while the Vernacular Press Act remained a feature of the Lytton era.

 

NOTE

 

• The annexation of Awadh in 1856 (Option 1): The annexation of Awadh in 1856 on the charge of misgovernance was one of the political causes and affected many sepoys who came from that region.

 

• The Doctrine of Lapse (Option 3): The Doctrine of Lapse was introduced by Dalhousie and was among the main political causes that made rulers like the Rani of Jhansi and Nana Sahib hostile.

 

• The greased cartridges of the Enfield rifle (Option 4): The greased cartridge episode of the Enfield rifle was the immediate cause that sparked the mutiny at Barrackpore and Meerut.

question: Consider the pairs of centre and leader of the Revolt of 1857. All pairs are correctly matched EXCEPT:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Delhi - Kunwar Singh.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Delhi was ruled symbolically by Bahadur Shah II with Bakht Khan as the real military head, whereas Kunwar Singh was the chief organiser in Bihar (दिल्ली - बहादुर शाह/बख्त खान, कुँवर सिंह - बिहार)

 

• Kanpur - Nana Sahib is correct, with Tantia Tope and Azimullah as his lieutenants.

 

• Lucknow - Begum Hazrat Mahal is correct; she led the revolt in Awadh.

 

• Jhansi - Rani Laxmi Bai is correct; she and Tantia Tope later captured Gwalior.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• Kunwar Singh's base was Jagdishpur near Arrah.

 

• Bakht Khan took charge of Delhi's rebel army after reaching the city from Bareilly.

 

• Peer Ali Khan was another rebel in the Bihar belt, active at Patna.

 

• Delhi's rebel court was led by the aged Bahadur Shah and the real strength came from Bakht Khan, whereas Kunwar Singh's fame comes from the Jagdishpur-Arrah belt of Bihar.

 

NOTE

 

• Kanpur - Nana Sahib (Option 1): Kanpur was indeed the centre led by Nana Sahib, the adopted son of Baji Rao II, with Tantia Tope as his commander, so this pair is correctly matched.

 

• Lucknow - Begum Hazrat Mahal (Option 2): Lucknow was the seat of the Begum of Awadh, who proclaimed her son Birjis Qadr as Nawab, so this is a correct pairing and not the exception.

 

• Jhansi - Rani Laxmi Bai (Option 4): Rani Laxmi Bai is rightly connected with Jhansi, from where she resisted Hugh Rose in 1858, hence this is a correct pair and cannot be the answer.

question: Among the military grievances of the Indian sepoys before 1857 was that they:
option_1: could not rise above the rank of Subedar
option_2: were allowed to rise to the rank of Colonel
option_3: received higher pay than European soldiers
option_4: were paid foreign allowance in all territories
solution_text:
The correct answer is could not rise above the rank of Subedar.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Indian soldiers had low salaries and poor prospects of promotion, and could not rise above the rank of Subedar (सूबेदार से ऊपर पदोन्नति नहीं)

 

• They were also denied the foreign allowance (batta) when serving in territories outside India, and the cartridge issue added to the sense of insult.

 

• They faced racial insults from European officers, which strengthened the feeling that the Company did not respect them.

 

• These grievances explain why the Bengal Army, rather than civilians, was the first to rise.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The highest rank open to Indians was Subedar, while all senior commands remained with Europeans.

 

• European soldiers received higher pay and better facilities than sepoys.

 

• The Bengal Army was dominated by high-caste soldiers from Awadh and Bihar.

 

• Pay of an Indian sepoy was about seven rupees a month at that time, whereas the European soldier was paid much more, and the racial gap in promotion was a key source of resentment.

 

NOTE

 

• were allowed to rise to the rank of Colonel (Option 2): Indians were barred from commissioned ranks like Colonel, which were reserved for European officers; the highest Indian rank was Subedar, so this statement is untrue.

 

• received higher pay than European soldiers (Option 3): European soldiers were paid more than Indian sepoys; the grievance was the low pay of the sepoys, so the claim that they received higher pay is wrong.

 

• were paid foreign allowance in all territories (Option 4): The sepoys were refused batta (foreign allowance) when serving outside India, so being paid it in all territories is the opposite of their grievance.

question: The allowance refused to the Indian sepoys when they served in foreign territory, which was a grievance before 1857, was called:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Batta.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Batta was the foreign allowance paid to soldiers on service abroad, and the Indian sepoys were refused it (विदेश सेवा भत्ता - बट्टा)

 

• Combined with poor pay, slow promotion, and racial insults, the denial of batta added to resentment in the Bengal Army.

 

• These grievances were the military causes of the Revolt.

 

• They contributed to the sepoys' willingness to act when the issue of greased cartridges struck their religious sentiments.

 

• Batta was thus a financial grievance of the army, and it joined the lack of promotion above Subedar and racial insult as a reason why the sepoys were unhappy even before the cartridge issue arose.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Batta also meant additional allowance given to the Company's officers in Bengal.

 

• Clive's reduction of double batta in 1766 had caused the White Mutiny.

 

• The general feeling in the army was that the Company could use sepoys for conquests overseas without extra pay.

 

• The word batta is used in Indian English also for allowances to employees on tour, and the sepoy's batta dispute in the Sind and Punjab campaigns annoyed the army before 1857.

 

NOTE

 

• Dastak (Option 1): Dastak was a trade permit that exempted Company servants from customs duties in eighteenth-century Bengal, and has no link with sepoys' allowances.

 

• Peshkash (Option 2): Peshkash refers to a tribute or present given by a subordinate chief to a superior authority, not to an allowance given to soldiers serving abroad.

 

• Chauth (Option 3): Chauth was the Maratha levy of one-fourth of the revenue on neighbouring territories, so it is unrelated to the military grievances of sepoys.

question: The Revolt of 1857, which began at Meerut, is said to have effectively concluded at:
solution_text:
The correct answer is Gwalior.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Sepoy Mutiny began at Meerut and effectively concluded at Gwalior in June 1858 after Hugh Rose recaptured the fort (विद्रोह मेरठ से शुरू होकर ग्वालियर में समाप्त हुआ)

 

• Rani Laxmi Bai and Tantia Tope had seized Gwalior, but Rose's army defeated them there, and the Rani died on 17 June 1858.

 

• Tantia Tope continued as a guerrilla leader until he was captured and hanged in 1859.

 

• Resistance in other regions such as Awadh and Rohilkhand had been put down earlier.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Revolt thus lasted a little over a year, from May 1857 to June 1858.

 

• Peace was formally proclaimed by Canning in July 1858.

 

• Gwalior's ruler Scindia was an ally of the British.

 

• The end is sometimes dated to 8 July 1858, when Canning declared peace, though small bands and leaders like Tantia Tope continued fighting until the capture and hanging in 1859.

 

NOTE

 

• Delhi (Option 2): Delhi fell to the British in September 1857, nine months before the final events at Gwalior, so it was not where the Revolt effectively ended.

 

• Lucknow (Option 3): Lucknow was relieved and recaptured by Colin Campbell by March 1858, before Gwalior was retaken in June, so the Revolt did not end there.

 

• Kanpur (Option 4): Kanpur was first recaptured by Havelock in July 1857 and secured by Colin Campbell in December 1857, long before the final conclusion of the Revolt at Gwalior in 1858.

question:
Consider the following statements about Mangal Pandey:

1. He was a sepoy of the 34th Bengal Native Infantry.

2. He killed Lt. Baugh and Sergeant-Major Hewson at Barrackpore.

3. He was hanged at Barrackpore on 8 April 1857.

Which of the statements given above are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 3 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: he served in the 34th Bengal Native Infantry at Barrackpore (मंगल पांडे 34वीं बंगाल नेटिव इन्फैंट्री में थे)

 

• Statement 2 is wrong: on 29 March 1857 he wounded Lt. Baugh and Sergeant-Major Hewson but did not kill any officer.

 

• Statement 3 is correct: he was hanged on 8 April 1857 at Barrackpore, and his regiment was disbanded.

 

• His action is described as the first major incident of the Sepoy Mutiny, though it was an individual act of defiance.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Meerut outbreak followed on 10 May 1857.

 

• Pandey's refusal came over the cartridges of the Enfield rifle.

 

• Other sepoys of his unit were punished and the regiment was disbanded.

 

• The regiment's punishment shows that the Company treated the matter as a mutiny, and disbanded sepoys carried tales of the incident to other garrisons, which helped the rumours travel.

 

NOTE

 

• 1 and 2 only (Option 1): This combination treats the claim that he killed the officers as true; he only wounded them, so statement 2 spoils the choice, though statement 1 is accurate.

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 2): Statement 1 about the regiment is true and statement 3 about the hanging is also true; the combination fails by wrongly relying on the claim of killing officers.

 

• 1, 2 and 3 (Option 4): Selecting all three would mean accepting that Mangal Pandey killed Lt. Baugh and Hewson, whereas he only wounded them, and statement 2 therefore makes this choice wrong.

question:
Consider the following statements about leaders of the Revolt of 1857:

1. Kunwar Singh was the chief organiser of the revolt in Bihar.

2. Khan Bahadur Khan led the rebels at Bareilly.

3. Maulavi Ahmadullah Shah led the rebels in the Mandla region of Madhya Pradesh.

Which of the statements given above is/are correct?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 1 and 2 only.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Statement 1 is correct: Kunwar Singh of Jagdishpur organised the revolt in Bihar (कुँवर सिंह - बिहार)

 

• Statement 2 is correct: Khan Bahadur Khan was the leader of the rising at Bareilly in Rohilkhand.

 

• Statement 3 is wrong: the Mandla region of Madhya Pradesh was the base of Rani Avantibai Lodhi, who raised an army of four thousand, while Maulavi Ahmadullah led the rebels at Faizabad.

 

• Therefore only statements 1 and 2 are correct.

 

• Bihar, Rohilkhand and Mandla lie in separate regions, which shows how the Revolt flared up in pockets under local leaders without any common command.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• Maulavi Ahmadullah Shah, a popular preacher of Faizabad, was killed in 1858.

 

• Rani Avantibai belonged to Ramgarh.

 

• Bareilly, Faizabad, Mandla and Bihar all appear in the list of centres of the revolt.

 

• The four centres of Bareilly, Faizabad, Mandla and Bihar show that the Revolt had local leaders, which also explains why it lacked a single command.

 

NOTE

 

• 2 and 3 only (Option 1): Statement 1 is correct, so dropping it is not right; and statement 3 wrongly gives Mandla to Maulavi Ahmadullah, who was active at Faizabad, which makes this pair of statements wrong.

 

• 1 and 3 only (Option 3): Statement 2 is true and so excluding it is a mistake; statement 3 attributes the Mandla region to Maulavi Ahmadullah, whereas it was the area of Rani Avantibai.

 

• 3 only (Option 4): Choosing statement 3 alone is incorrect since it names the wrong leader for Mandla, and two true statements about Kunwar Singh and Khan Bahadur Khan are left out.

question:
Assertion (A): The rebel sepoys at Meerut marched to Delhi and proclaimed Bahadur Shah II as emperor.

Reason (R): The Mughal emperor in Delhi still held a symbolic authority that could unite the rebels.
option_1: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_2: A is true but R is false
option_3: A is false but R is true
option_4: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Assertion A is true: after the Meerut rising on 10 May 1857, the sepoys went to Delhi and on 12 May proclaimed Bahadur Shah II as Shahenshah-e-Hindustan (मेरठ के सिपाही दिल्ली पहुँचे)

 

• Reason R is true: the aged Mughal king was only a nominal ruler, but the dynasty's name still carried prestige among Hindus and Muslims alike.

 

• R explains A: the rebels wanted a legitimate head around whom different groups could rally, and so they turned to the Mughal emperor in Delhi.

 

• Real control in Delhi rested with his army general Bakht Khan.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• Delhi was recaptured by John Nicholson's forces on 20 September 1857.

 

• Bahadur Shah was later deported to Rangoon.

 

• The emperor's seat in the Red Fort was the symbolic focus of the rising.

 

• The assertion-reason pattern in 1857 questions tests whether a cause explains an outcome, and in Delhi's case the Mughal title helped the rebels give their rising a recognised leader.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 1): The reason is not just a related fact but the actual reason why the rebels turned to the emperor; the Mughal throne's symbolic authority explains the proclamation, so it is the correct explanation.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 2): The assertion is true, as the sepoys did march to Delhi and proclaim Bahadur Shah II; the choice that calls it false is therefore wrong.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 3): The reason is true because the Mughal emperor's name still commanded respect; saying the reason is true while the assertion is false contradicts the recorded events of May 1857.

question:
Assertion (A): The use of greased cartridges angered both Hindu and Muslim sepoys.

Reason (R): The grease was rumoured to be made from beef and pig fat.
option_1: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_2: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_3: A is true but R is false
option_4: A is false but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Assertion A is true: the cartridges of the new Enfield rifle offended Hindu and Muslim soldiers alike (हिंदू और मुस्लिम दोनों सिपाही नाराज़ हुए)

 

• Reason R is true: the grease was said to contain beef and pig fat, and the cartridge had to be bitten with the mouth.

 

• R explains A: beef is forbidden to Hindus, and pork to Muslims, so the rumour hurt both groups.

 

• The sepoys believed the government was deliberately trying to destroy their religion and cultural identity.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

 

Additional Information

 

• The refusal first occurred at Berhampur and Barrackpore.

 

• The incident was the immediate cause and not the only cause.

 

• Both Hindus and Muslims took part in the Revolt, which is seen as a sign of unity.

 

• The sepoys' fear of defilement was reinforced by earlier rumours that flour had been mixed with bone dust, an idea that spread through chapatis and other symbolic circulation in early 1857.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 2): The reason supplies exactly why the two communities were angry, so denying that it explains the assertion is incorrect; the rumour of beef and pig fat was the heart of the grievance.

 

• A is true but R is false (Option 3): The reason is true, as the grease was believed to be of beef and pig fat, so calling it false is not correct for the greased-cartridge episode.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 4): The assertion is true as both communities were hurt by the cartridges, and the option claiming it is false ignores the shared religious grievance of Hindu and Muslim soldiers.

question:
Assertion (A): The Revolt of 1857 failed to dislodge British rule.

Reason (R): The rebels had a single unified plan, a central command and modern weapons superior to the British.
option_1: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
option_2: A is true but R is false
option_3: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
option_4: A is false but R is true
solution_text:
The correct answer is A is true but R is false.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Assertion A is true: the Revolt was ultimately unsuccessful, and in 1858 Company rule ended and Crown rule began (विद्रोह अंततः असफल रहा)

 

• Reason R is false: the rebels lacked a unified plan and central leadership, as leaders such as Nana Sahib, Hazrat Mahal and Kunwar Singh fought in separate regions.

 

• The British had better weapons, the telegraph, and reinforcements, and Sikh, Gurkha and many princely forces stayed loyal.

 

• So the correct choice is that the assertion is true but the reason is false.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Revolt was largely confined to north and central India.

 

• Delhi fell in September 1857, Lucknow in March 1858 and Gwalior in June 1858.

 

• After 1858 the army was reorganised, with more European troops.

 

• The British also benefited from railways and the telegraph, built under Dalhousie, which let them move troops and news faster than the rebels could communicate.

 

NOTE

 

• Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A (Option 1): The reason is false, so the pair cannot be both true; the rebels had no common plan or modern weaponry, and so R cannot explain why the Revolt failed.

 

• Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A (Option 3): Even if A is true, R is false because the rebels were poorly equipped and divided, so describing R as true though not explanatory is also wrong.

 

• A is false but R is true (Option 4): The assertion is true because the Revolt was suppressed by 1858, so the claim that A is false while R is true gets both statements the wrong way round.

question: Which of the following was a significant importance of the Revolt of 1857?
option_1: It led to the formation of the Indian National Congress in 1858
option_2: It established the Supreme Court of India
option_3: It fostered patriotism and promoted Hindu-Muslim unity
option_4: It ended the British East India Company in 1757
solution_text:
The correct answer is It fostered patriotism and promoted Hindu-Muslim unity.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• The Revolt, though unsuccessful, fostered patriotism among the people and brought Hindus and Muslims together in a common struggle (विद्रोह ने देशभक्ति और हिंदू-मुस्लिम एकता को बढ़ाया)

 

• Hindu and Muslim sepoys and chiefs fought side by side under leaders such as Bahadur Shah Zafar and Nana Sahib.

 

• It forced the British to end Company rule, abolish the Doctrine of Lapse and promise non-interference in religion.

 

• Its memory inspired later nationalists and later movements, including Savarkar's reading of it as a war of independence.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

 

Additional Information

 

• The Congress was founded in 1885 by A.O. Hume.

 

• The British later adopted a policy of 'divide and rule'.

 

• The Revolt is also called the Sepoy Mutiny and the Great Rebellion.

 

• Other results include the reorganised Indian army with a higher share of European troops and artillery kept under British control, and a policy of balancing castes and communities in regiments.

 

NOTE

 

• It led to the formation of the Indian National Congress in 1858 (Option 1): The Indian National Congress was founded in 1885, not in 1858, by A.O. Hume and others, so this option fails by placing it right after the Revolt.

 

• It established the Supreme Court of India (Option 2): The Supreme Court of India came into existence in 1950 with the Constitution; the Revolt did not establish it, although the notes mention the Supreme Court in the context of social grievances.

 

• It ended the British East India Company in 1757 (Option 4): The Company ended in 1858, not in 1757; 1757 is the year of Plassey, which began British political power in Bengal, so the date given is wrong.

question: What was the fate of Tantia Tope after the Revolt of 1857 was suppressed in central India?
option_2: He was betrayed, captured and hanged by the British
option_3: He died fighting at the fort of Jhansi
option_4: He was pardoned and made a Deputy Collector
solution_text:
The correct answer is He was betrayed, captured and hanged by the British.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Tantia Tope was captured and hanged by the British in April 1859, after being betrayed by a friend and defeated by Hugh Rose (तात्या टोपे को पकड़कर फाँसी दी गई)

 

• He had been the commander of Nana Sahib at Kanpur and had fought alongside Rani Laxmi Bai in the Gwalior campaign.

 

• After the fall of Gwalior he resorted to guerrilla warfare in central India for about ten months.

 

• His hanging effectively ended organised resistance by the Revolt's leaders.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

 

Additional Information

 

• His real name was Ramchandra Pandurang Tope.

 

• The Rani of Jhansi died before him, in June 1858.

 

• Nana Sahib vanished into Nepal.

 

• Nobody knows exactly where Nana Sahib himself went after 1858, with most accounts saying he escaped into Nepal, which explains why the hanging of Tantia Tope was viewed as final.

 

NOTE

 

• He was deported to Rangoon (Option 1): Deportation to Rangoon was the fate of Bahadur Shah Zafar, the last Mughal emperor, in 1858; Tantia Tope was executed instead.

 

• He died fighting at the fort of Jhansi (Option 3): Tantia Tope did not die at Jhansi; it was Rani Laxmi Bai who died as a soldier in June 1858, after the fighting at Jhansi and Gwalior.

 

• He was pardoned and made a Deputy Collector (Option 4): He was not pardoned or given an official post, because the British tried him and executed him in 1859, unlike some who surrendered under the amnesty.

question: Rani Laxmi Bai of Jhansi, who died a soldier's death in 1858, was popularly known by which childhood nickname?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Manu.

 

IMPORTANT POINTS

 

• Rani Laxmi Bai, born Manikarnika, was known by the nickname Manu, and she married Raja Gangadhar Rao of Jhansi (रानी लक्ष्मीबाई का उपनाम मनु था)

 

• The couple adopted a child in 1853, but the British applied the Doctrine of Lapse, refused recognition and annexed Jhansi.

 

• She joined the rebels, resisted Hugh Rose's assault on Jhansi in April 1858, and later captured Gwalior with Tantia Tope.

 

• She died fighting on 17 June 1858 and is remembered as a symbol of resistance.

 

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

 

Additional Information

 

• She was brought up at Bithur in the household of Nana Sahib, with whom she shared lessons in horse-riding and swordsmanship.

 

• The poem by Subhadra Kumari Chauhan describes her as a heroine.

 

• Her adopted son Damodar Rao was formerly Anand Rao.

 

• Jhansi was seized by Hugh Rose in April 1858 after a two-week siege, and the Rani escaped on horseback with her adopted son to Kalpi and later to Gwalior.

 

NOTE

 

• Gauri (Option 1): Gauri is a name for the goddess Parvati and was not a nickname of the Rani of Jhansi, who was called Manu in childhood.

 

• Radha (Option 2): Radha is the name of Krishna's beloved in the Bhakti tradition; the Rani's family called her Manu, so this name does not fit.

 

• Padmini (Option 3): Padmini is the legendary queen of Chittor who performed jauhar, a historical figure of the medieval age, not a nickname of Laxmi Bai.
